en: When sending prompts to Codex, you can send
them like this, as we also did before for
editing the spec file. But if you're not
sure if Codex has all the context it needs
to execute this task in the best possible
way, or if you're not sure if it will really
execute the task in the way you want it to,
it is a good idea to switch to plan mode,
which you can do here in the app by using
the plus and plan mode or by using
Command+Shift+P
or just
Shift+Tab. That switches to plan mode as you
can see down here. In the IDE integration,
you can also use plan mode like this
or Shift+Tab. And the same is true for the
CLI. Shift+Tab switches you to plan mode
there and Shift+Tab again switches you out
of it.
Now in plan mode, Codex will ask you
follow-up questions if it needs more
information. It will not always ask
questions, but if it needs more information,
it will do so. And it will make a plan which
you can review and change before it goes to
work.
So here I'll send this prompt in plan mode,
and now it'll again
go through the project, try to find relevant
context, explore the spec.md file,
think about the task, and then make a plan
and share that with you before it continues.
I'll also start it here in plan mode in the
CLI just so that you see both in action.
I'll then finish the task in only of these
apps though.
Now here in the CLI, it already has a
follow-up question
whether I want to use grouped layouts or
flat app routes.
And I indeed wanna use grouped layouts,
let's say.
And I also want it to add these loading.tsx
and error.tsx files, which are a Next.js
feature for showing a loading screen or an
error fallback screen if things go wrong.
Now even with confirming that, it doesn't
yet start working. It'll just include that
into its plan.
It got the same questions as it seems here
in
the
native app,
though here it also has another question and
I'll confirm that. And now I got a plan here
in the CLI which I can
analyze and of course which I can tweak with
follow-up prompts.
So if I'm not happy about something, I can
tell it to no, stay in plan mode and then
tell it what should change or if I'm happy,
I can use yes here, and that will then
automatically switch it out of plan mode and
it will start working and it'll be able to
edit the files because in plan mode, it's
not able to edit or create files. It's just
able to read them, to gather information and
make that plan.
Same here in the native app, of course. And
I can now analyze the plan there too. And
you should analyze it. I know many
developers just blindly accept it. And in
that case, plan mode is better than nothing,
but really, analyze this plan and tell it to
change things you don't like. This plan is
the blueprint for how it's going to
implement your task and therefore you should
make sure your plan is good. Here I
specifically like this part, for example,
which is important for Next.js to
not unnecessarily convert components into
client-side components, which could have
disadvantages for search engine optimization
or performance. But I do indeed have one
follow-up here. So I'll choose no and tell
it what to do differently because I want to
make sure that it does share and reuse
general and other components and store them
in a source components folder.
And I'll then submit this to have it create
an updated plan. And we could have done the
same here in the CLI or IDE integration, of
course. So here's the updated plan or it's
just getting written
and I'll now choose yes, implement this plan
or just use submit or the shortcut. And have
it start working on that plan.
So here I now got a permission popup because
I'm of course running in that default
permissions mode. So not all
actions are possible by default.
Here it wants to run bun run build to build
this project for production to see if there
are any errors.
And I'm fine with that also in general. So
I'll choose the second option to in general
allow it to run bun run build also in the
future so that it won't ask again for this
kind of permission. And now it's done. And
therefore what I'll do
is I'll start my development server using
Bun,
which of course must be installed therefore.
And then I can visit localhost:3000, which
is the default port for this dev server. I
can see my dummy starting page and we can
also try visiting some other routes like
/login/register.
And I'm doing that here,
also a dummy share route.
Which also works, and also the notes routes
if we want to. So that all seems to work.
And if I enter some route that should not be
supported, I get a 404 page. So that all
looks decent.
